title-group.article-title: Ophelia yangi sp. nov. (Annelida, Opheliidae), a new species from Chinese waters, with comments on the taxonomic characters of the genus

abstract.label: Abstract
abstract.p: Ophelia limacina (Rathke, 1843), originally described from Norway, is the only species of Ophelia Savigny, 1822 recorded from Chinese waters, but these records have never been verified. To clarify the identity of the Chinese Ophelia, specimens from the Chinese coast, from Shandong to Fujian, were examined. They differ from O. limacina and from all other congeners and are described here as Ophelia yangisp. nov.; the earlier Yellow Sea record of O. cf. limacina is also tentatively referred to the new species. The new species has 32 chaetigers with the body formula 10a + 16b + 6a, i.e., ten anterior abranchiate, 16 branchiate, and six posterior abranchiate chaetigers, and simple cirriform branchiae; branchial fenestrations are present. The body formula was constant in all specimens examined, except on one side of one of 20 specimens. In the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) and 16S rRNA genes, the new species differs from all other sequenced taxa of Ophelia by uncorrected p-distances of 15.6–16.5% (COI) and 6.4–7.8% (16S), whereas the maximum intraspecific COI distance is 0.5%. The variation observed in the examined specimens was used to evaluate the characters that have been used to distinguish species of Ophelia. The body formula was stable in these specimens, whereas the length of the branchiae, the posterior dorsal longitudinal ridges, the origin of the ventral groove, and the nephridiopores varied among specimens or were difficult to observe in preserved material; these characters should therefore be used with caution.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ophelia Savigny, 1822 (Opheliidae Malmgren, 1867) currently comprises 37 valid species (Read and Fauchald 2026). Its species are deposit feeders that live mainly in clean sandy sediments (Bellan and Dauvin 1991; Blake and Maciolek 2020). Most of them have been described from temperate waters: 18 from the North Atlantic and the Mediterranean, five from western and southern Africa, five from southern Australia, three from the northeastern Pacific, three from South America, and one from the Southern Ocean. Only two species have been described from the tropical Indo-West Pacific, and none from the Northwest Pacific (Fig. 1). Because the external morphology of the genus is rather uniform, species are distinguished mainly by the body formula, i.e., the numbers of anterior abranchiate, branchiate and posterior abranchiate chaetigers (Tebble 1952, 1953; Bellan and Dauvin 1991). Other characters, such as the posterior dorsal longitudinal ridges (e.g., Fauvel 1927; Tebble 1952), the origin of the ventral groove (e.g., Monro 1936; Gibbs 1971; Bellan 1975) and the number of anal papillae (e.g., Gibbs 1971; Hartmann-Schröder and Parker 1995), have also been used to separate species.

Ophelia limacina was described from Norway (Rathke 1843) and has long been reported from the Arctic, the North Atlantic, the northeastern Pacific, and Japan (Bellan and Dauvin 1991). This broad concept, however, has been increasingly questioned. Tebble (1952) found that British Museum (Natural History) specimens labelled O. limacina included other species. He reinstated O. borealis Quatrefages, 1866 and O. rathkei McIntosh, 1908, both previously treated as synonyms, and suggested that O. limacina does not occur in British waters. Bellan and Dauvin (1991) later suggested that O. limacina may represent a species complex, and COI barcoding revealed two divergent lineages among Canadian specimens identified under this name (Carr et al. 2011). These findings warrant re-examination of Northwest Pacific records of O. limacina, far from its Norwegian type locality.

During recent macrobenthic surveys along the coasts of Fujian and Zhejiang provinces, China, we collected specimens of Ophelia from intertidal sandy beaches in Quanzhou and the subtidal zone off Wenzhou, and we also examined a specimen collected in 1983 at Jiaonan, Shandong Province. These specimens have fewer chaetigers and branchiae than O. limacina (10 anterior abranchiate, 16 branchiate, and six posterior abranchiate chaetigers, vs 10, 23, and four in the original description; Rathke 1843), suggesting that they represent an undescribed species. To test this hypothesis, we examined their morphology in detail. As additional evidence, we obtained sequences of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) and 16S rRNA genes by genome skimming (Yang et al. 2024) and compared them with those of congeners available in GenBank. Here we describe Ophelia yangi sp. nov., compare it with O. limacina and with its morphologically closest congeners, and, based on the variation observed in our specimens and in the literature, comment on the characters used to distinguish species of Ophelia.
